#### Fractional factorial example {#sec-pri-472}

[**A "Catapult" Fractional Factorial Experiment**]{#sec-pri-472-overview}

**A step-by-step analysis of a fractional factorial "catapult" experiment**

This experiment was conducted by a team of students on a catapult, a table-top wooden device used to teach design of experiments and statistical process control. The catapult has several controllable factors and a response easily measured in a classroom setting. It has been used for over 10 years in hundreds of classes.

[**Description of Experiment: Response and Factors**]{#sec-pri-472-description}

**The experiment has five factors that might affect the distance the golf ball travels**

*Purpose*: To determine the significant factors that affect the distance the ball is thrown by the catapult, and to determine the settings required to reach three different distances (30, 60 and 90 inches).

*Response Variable*: The distance in inches from the front of the catapult to the spot where the ball lands. The ball is a plastic golf ball.

*Number of observations:* 20 (a $2^{5-1}$ resolution V design with 4 center points).

*Variables*:

1. Response Variable $Y$ = distance
2. Factor 1 = band height (height of the pivot point for the rubber bands, levels were 2.25 and 4.75 inches with a centerpoint level of 3.5)
3. Factor 2 = start angle (location of the arm when the operator releases, starts the forward motion of the arm, levels were 0 and 20 degrees with a centerpoint level of 10 degrees)
4. Factor 3 = rubber bands (number of rubber bands used on the catapult, levels were 1 and 2 bands)
5. Factor 4 = arm length (distance the arm is extended, levels were 0 and 4 inches with a centerpoint level of 2 inches)
6. Factor 5 = stop angle (location of the arm where the forward motion of the arm is stopped and the ball starts flying, levels were 45 and 80 degrees with a centerpoint level of 62 degrees)

::: {.callout-note}
NIST's page states the band height levels as 2.25 and 4.75 inches with a centerpoint of 3.5. The archived data file (`CATAPULT.DAT`) that NIST's own page links to instead records 3.25, 4.00, and 4.75 inches for the low, center, and high band-height settings. We reproduce NIST's stated levels here (per our verbatim-fidelity convention for descriptive prose), but use the actual recorded values from `CATAPULT.DAT` throughout the analysis below, since those are what the response was actually measured against.
:::

[**Design matrix and responses (in run order)**]{#sec-pri-472-data}

The design matrix appears below in (randomized) run order. The reader can download the data as a [text file](../../datasets/CATAPULT.DAT).

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| label: setup-pri-472
#| message: false
library(tidyverse)
library(patchwork)
theme_set(theme_light())

catapult <- read_table(
  here::here("datasets", "CATAPULT.DAT"),
  skip = 50,
  col_names = c("distance", "height", "start", "bands", "length", "stop",
                "h", "s", "b", "l", "e", "order", "cent", "pattern"),
  col_types = "ddddddddddddic"
)

catapult |>
  select(distance, height, start, bands, length, stop, order) |>
  arrange(order)
```

**One discrete factor**

Note that four of the factors are continuous, and one, number of rubber bands, is discrete. Due to the presence of this discrete factor, we actually have two different centerpoints, each with two runs. Runs 7 and 19 are with one rubber band, and the center of the other factors, while runs 2 and 13 are with two rubber bands and the center of the other factors.

**Five confirmatory runs**

After analyzing the 20 runs and determining factor settings needed to achieve predicted distances of 30, 60 and 90 inches, the team was asked to conduct five confirmatory runs at each of the derived settings.

[**Analysis of the Experiment**]{#sec-pri-472-analysis}

**Step 1: Look at the data**

We start by plotting the data several ways to see if any trends or anomalies appear that would not be accounted for by the models.

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| label: fig-pri-472-4plot
#| fig-cap: "4-plot of the catapult distance response (center points highlighted)"
p1 <- ggplot(catapult, aes(sample = distance)) +
  stat_qq(distribution = qnorm) +
  stat_qq_line(distribution = qnorm, color = "#D60021") +
  labs(title = "Normal Probability Plot", x = "Normal Quantile", y = "Distance")

p2 <- ggplot(catapult, aes(x = "", y = distance)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "#DCE6F1") +
  labs(title = "Box Plot", x = NULL, y = "Distance")

p3 <- ggplot(catapult, aes(x = distance)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 9, fill = "#DCE6F1", color = "#1B1B1B") +
  labs(title = "Histogram", x = "Distance", y = "Frequency")

p4 <- ggplot(catapult, aes(x = order, y = distance)) +
  geom_line(color = "steelblue", alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_point(aes(color = cent > 0), size = 2) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = "#D60021", `FALSE` = "steelblue"), guide = "none") +
  labs(title = "Run-Order Plot", x = "Run Order", y = "Distance")

(p1 + p2) / (p3 + p4)
```

We can see the large spread of the data and a pattern to the data that should be explained by the analysis. The run order plot does not indicate an obvious time sequence. The four highlighted points in the run order plot are the center points in the design. Recall that runs 2 and 13 had two rubber bands and runs 7 and 19 had one rubber band. There may be a slight aging of the rubber bands in that the second center point resulted in a distance that was a little shorter than the first for each pair.

*Plots of responses versus factor columns*

Next look at the plots of responses sorted by factor columns.

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| label: fig-pri-472-boxfactors
#| fig-cap: "Distance by factor level"
factor_labels_raw <- c(height = "Band Height", start = "Start Angle", bands = "Number of Bands",
                        length = "Arm Length", stop = "Stop Angle")

catapult_long <- catapult |>
  pivot_longer(c(height, start, bands, length, stop), names_to = "factor", values_to = "level") |>
  mutate(factor = factor(factor_labels_raw[factor], levels = factor_labels_raw))

ggplot(catapult_long, aes(factor(level), distance)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "#DCE6F1") +
  facet_wrap(~factor, scales = "free_x", nrow = 2) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Distance")
```

Several factors appear to change the average response level and most have large spread at each of the levels.

**Step 2: Create the theoretical model**

With a resolution V design we are able to estimate all the main effects and all two-factor interactions without worrying about confounding. Therefore, the initial model will have 16 terms: the intercept term, the 5 main effects, and the 10 two-factor interactions.

**Step 3: Create the actual model from the data**

*Variable coding*

Note we have used the orthogonally coded columns for the analysis, and have abbreviated the factor names as follows: Height (`h`) = band height, Start (`s`) = start angle, Bands (`b`) = number of rubber bands, Stop (`e`) = stop angle, Length (`l`) = arm length.

*Trial model with all main factors and two-factor interactions*

The results of fitting the trial model that includes all main factors and two-factor interactions follow.

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| label: pri-472-full-model
full_fit <- lm(
  distance ~ h + s + b + l + e +
    h:s + h:b + h:l + h:e + s:b + s:l + s:e + b:l + b:e + l:e,
  data = catapult
)
summary(full_fit)
```

This reproduces NIST's reported summary of fit exactly: $R^2 = 0.9709$, adjusted $R^2 = 0.8619$, and residual standard error $= 13.28$ on 4 degrees of freedom.

*Use p-values and a normal probability plot to help select significant effects*

The model has a good $R^2$ value, but the fact that $R^2$ adjusted is considerably smaller indicates that we undoubtedly have some terms in our model that are not significant. Scanning the column of $p$-values (labeled `Pr(>|t|)`) for small values shows five significant effects at the 0.05 level and another one at the 0.10 level.

A normal probability plot of effects is a useful graphical tool to determine significant effects. The graph below shows that there are nine terms in the model that can be assumed to be noise. That would leave six terms to be included in the model. Whereas the output above shows a $p$-value of 0.0836 for the interaction of Bands (`b`) and Length (`l`), the normal plot suggests we treat this interaction as significant.

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| label: fig-pri-472-normaleffects
#| fig-cap: "Normal probability plot of the main effects and interactions"
effects_df <- broom::tidy(full_fit) |>
  filter(term != "(Intercept)") |>
  mutate(effect = 2 * estimate, term_label = str_replace_all(term, ":", "*")) |>
  arrange(effect) |>
  mutate(rank = row_number(), qnorm_score = qnorm((rank - 0.5) / n()))

sig_terms <- c("h", "s", "b", "l", "e", "b*l")
effects_df <- effects_df |> mutate(significant = term_label %in% sig_terms)

line_fit <- lm(effect ~ qnorm_score, data = effects_df)

ggplot(effects_df, aes(qnorm_score, effect)) +
  geom_abline(intercept = coef(line_fit)[1], slope = coef(line_fit)[2], color = "steelblue") +
  geom_point(aes(color = significant), size = 2) +
  ggrepel::geom_text_repel(
    data = filter(effects_df, significant),
    aes(label = term_label), size = 3, seed = 1
  ) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = "#D60021", `FALSE` = "#1B1B1B"), guide = "none") +
  labs(x = "Normal Quantile", y = "Effect")
```

*Refit using just the effects that appear to matter*

Remove the non-significant terms from the model and refit to produce the following analysis of variance table.

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| label: pri-472-6term-model
fit6 <- lm(distance ~ h + s + b + l + e + b:l, data = catapult)
anova(fit6)
```

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| label: pri-472-6term-lof
resid6 <- residuals(fit6)
pe_groups <- catapult |>
  mutate(r = resid6) |>
  filter(cent > 0) |>
  group_by(cent) |>
  summarise(ss = sum((r - mean(r))^2), n = n(), .groups = "drop")

pure_error_ss <- sum(pe_groups$ss)
pure_error_df <- sum(pe_groups$n - 1)
resid_ss <- sum(resid6^2)
resid_df <- fit6$df.residual
lof_ss <- resid_ss - pure_error_ss
lof_df <- resid_df - pure_error_df
lof_ms <- lof_ss / lof_df
pe_ms <- pure_error_ss / pure_error_df
lof_F <- lof_ms / pe_ms
lof_p <- pf(lof_F, lof_df, pure_error_df, lower.tail = FALSE)

tibble(
  source = c("Lack-of-fit", "Pure error"),
  df = c(lof_df, pure_error_df),
  sum_sq = c(lof_ss, pure_error_ss),
  mean_sq = c(lof_ms, pe_ms),
  F_value = c(lof_F, NA),
  p_value = c(lof_p, NA)
)
```

The pure-error sum of squares comes from the two replicated centerpoint pairs (runs 7/19 with one rubber band, and runs 2/13 with two rubber bands). This reproduces NIST's reported lack-of-fit table exactly: lack-of-fit sum of squares $= 1973.74$ on 11 degrees of freedom, pure error $= 133.25$ on 2 degrees of freedom, $F = 2.69$, $p = 0.3018$.

*$R^2$ is OK and there is no significant model "lack of fit"*

The $R^2$ and $R^2$ adjusted values are acceptable. The ANOVA table shows us that the model is significant, and the lack-of-fit test is not significant. Parameter estimates are below.

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| label: pri-472-6term-summary
summary(fit6)
```

This reproduces NIST's reported summary exactly: $R^2 = 0.9131$, adjusted $R^2 = 0.873$, residual standard error $= 12.73$ on 13 degrees of freedom.

**Step 4: Test the model assumptions using residual graphs (adjust and simplify as needed)**

*Diagnostic residual plots*

To examine the assumption that the residuals are approximately normally distributed, are independent, and have equal variances, we generate four plots of the residuals: a normal probability plot, box plot, histogram, and a run-order plot of the residuals. In the run-order plot, the highlighted points are the centerpoint values.

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| label: fig-pri-472-resid1-4plot
#| fig-cap: "4-plot of the residuals, 6-term model"
resid_4plot <- function(df, resid_col, order_col = "order", cent_col = "cent") {
  p1 <- ggplot(df, aes(sample = .data[[resid_col]])) +
    stat_qq(distribution = qnorm) +
    stat_qq_line(distribution = qnorm, color = "#D60021") +
    labs(title = "Normal Probability Plot", x = "Normal Quantile", y = "Residual")
  p2 <- ggplot(df, aes(x = "", y = .data[[resid_col]])) +
    geom_boxplot(fill = "#DCE6F1") +
    labs(title = "Box Plot", x = NULL, y = "Residual")
  p3 <- ggplot(df, aes(x = .data[[resid_col]])) +
    geom_histogram(bins = 9, fill = "#DCE6F1", color = "#1B1B1B") +
    labs(title = "Histogram", x = "Residual", y = "Frequency")
  p4 <- ggplot(df, aes(x = .data[[order_col]], y = .data[[resid_col]])) +
    geom_line(color = "steelblue", alpha = 0.4) +
    geom_point(aes(color = .data[[cent_col]] > 0), size = 2) +
    scale_color_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = "#D60021", `FALSE` = "steelblue"), guide = "none") +
    labs(title = "Run-Order Plot", x = "Run Order", y = "Residual")
  (p1 + p2) / (p3 + p4)
}

catapult <- catapult |> mutate(resid6 = resid6, fitted6 = fitted(fit6))
resid_4plot(catapult, "resid6")
```

The residuals do appear to have, at least approximately, a normal distribution.

*Plot of residuals versus predicted values*

Next we plot the residuals versus the predicted values.

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| label: fig-pri-472-resid1-vspred
#| fig-cap: "Residuals versus predicted distance, 6-term model"
ggplot(catapult, aes(fitted6, resid6)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "gray60") +
  geom_point(color = "steelblue") +
  labs(x = "Predicted Distance", y = "Residual")
```

There does not appear to be a pattern to the residuals. One observation about the graph, from a single point, is that the model performs poorly in predicting a short distance. In fact, run number 10 had a measured distance of 8 inches, but the model predicts a negative distance, giving a large residual. The fact that the model predicts an impossible negative distance is an obvious shortcoming of the model. We may not be successful at predicting the catapult settings required to hit a distance less than 25 inches. This is not surprising since there is only one data value less than 28 inches. Recall that the objective is to achieve distances of 30, 60, and 90 inches.

*Plots of residuals versus the factor variables*

Next we look at the residual values versus each of the factors.

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| label: fig-pri-472-resid1-byfactor
#| fig-cap: "Residuals by factor, 6-term model"
factor_labels_coded <- c(h = "Band Height", s = "Start Angle", b = "Number of Bands",
                          l = "Arm Length", e = "Stop Angle")

catapult |>
  pivot_longer(c(h, s, b, l, e), names_to = "factor", values_to = "level") |>
  mutate(factor = factor(factor_labels_coded[factor], levels = factor_labels_coded)) |>
  ggplot(aes(level, resid6)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "gray60") +
  geom_point(color = "steelblue") +
  facet_wrap(~factor, nrow = 2) +
  labs(x = "Coded Factor Level", y = "Residual")
```

Most of the residual graphs versus the factors appear to have a slight "frown" on the graph (higher residuals in the center). This may indicate a lack of fit, or sign of curvature at the centerpoint values. The lack-of-fit test, however, indicates that the lack of fit is not significant.

*Consider a transformation of the response variable to see if we can obtain a better model*

At this point, since there are several unsatisfactory features of the model we have fit and the resultant residuals, we should consider whether a simple transformation of the response variable ($Y$ = "Distance") might improve the situation.

There are at least two good reasons to suspect that using the logarithm of distance as the response might lead to a better model.

1. A linear model fit to $\ln(Y)$ will always predict a positive distance when converted back to the original scale for any possible combination of $X$ factor values.
2. Physical considerations suggest that a realistic model for distance might require quadratic terms since gravity plays a key role -- taking logarithms often reduces the impact of non-linear terms.

To see whether using $\ln(Y)$ as the response leads to a more satisfactory model, we return to step 3.

**Step 3a: Fit the full model using ln(Y) as the response**

*First a main effects and two-factor interaction model is fit to the log distance responses*

Proceeding as before, using the coded values of the factor levels and the natural logarithm of distance as the response, we obtain the following parameter estimates.

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| label: pri-472-full-log-model
catapult <- catapult |> mutate(log_distance = log(distance))

full_log_fit <- lm(
  log_distance ~ h + s + b + l + e +
    h:s + h:b + h:l + h:e + s:b + s:l + s:e + b:l + b:e + l:e,
  data = catapult
)
summary(full_log_fit)
```

This reproduces NIST's reported summary exactly: $R^2 = 0.9564$, adjusted $R^2 = 0.7927$, residual standard error $= 0.307$ on 4 degrees of freedom.

*A simpler model with just main effects has a satisfactory fit*

Examining the $p$-values of the 16 model coefficients, only the intercept and the 5 main effect terms appear significant. Refitting the model with just these terms yields the following results.

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| label: pri-472-main-log-model
main_log_fit <- lm(log_distance ~ h + s + b + l + e, data = catapult)
anova(main_log_fit)
summary(main_log_fit)
```

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| label: pri-472-main-log-lof
resid_log <- residuals(main_log_fit)
pe_groups_log <- catapult |>
  mutate(r = resid_log) |>
  filter(cent > 0) |>
  group_by(cent) |>
  summarise(ss = sum((r - mean(r))^2), n = n(), .groups = "drop")

pure_error_ss_log <- sum(pe_groups_log$ss)
pure_error_df_log <- sum(pe_groups_log$n - 1)
resid_ss_log <- sum(resid_log^2)
resid_df_log <- main_log_fit$df.residual
lof_ss_log <- resid_ss_log - pure_error_ss_log
lof_df_log <- resid_df_log - pure_error_df_log
lof_ms_log <- lof_ss_log / lof_df_log
pe_ms_log <- pure_error_ss_log / pure_error_df_log
lof_F_log <- lof_ms_log / pe_ms_log
lof_p_log <- pf(lof_F_log, lof_df_log, pure_error_df_log, lower.tail = FALSE)

tibble(
  source = c("Lack-of-fit", "Pure error"),
  df = c(lof_df_log, pure_error_df_log),
  sum_sq = c(lof_ss_log, pure_error_ss_log),
  mean_sq = c(lof_ms_log, pe_ms_log),
  F_value = c(lof_F_log, NA),
  p_value = c(lof_p_log, NA)
)
```

This is a simpler model than previously obtained in Step 3 (no interaction term). All the terms are highly significant and there is no indication of a significant lack of fit: our lack-of-fit sum of squares ($0.590$ on 12 degrees of freedom) and pure error ($0.029$ on 2 degrees of freedom) reproduce NIST's reported $F = 3.371$, $p = 0.2514$ exactly.

We next look at the residuals for this new model fit.

**Step 4a: Test the (new) model assumptions using residual graphs (adjust and simplify as needed)**

*Normal probability plot, box plot, histogram, and run-order plot of the residuals*

The following normal plot, box plot, histogram and run-order plot of the residuals shows no problems.

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| label: fig-pri-472-resid2-4plot
#| fig-cap: "4-plot of the residuals, main-effects model on log distance"
catapult <- catapult |> mutate(resid_log = resid_log, fitted_log = fitted(main_log_fit))
resid_4plot(catapult, "resid_log")
```

Residuals plotted versus run order again show a possible slight decreasing trend (rubber band fatigue?).

*Plot of residuals versus predicted ln(Y) values*

A plot of the residuals versus the predicted $\ln(Y)$ values looks reasonable, although there might be a tendency for the model to overestimate slightly for high predicted values.

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| label: fig-pri-472-resid2-vspred
#| fig-cap: "Residuals versus predicted log distance"
ggplot(catapult, aes(fitted_log, resid_log)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "gray60") +
  geom_point(color = "steelblue") +
  labs(x = "Predicted log(Distance)", y = "Residual")
```

*Plot of residuals versus the factor variables*

Next we look at the residual values versus each of the factors.

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| label: fig-pri-472-resid2-byfactor
#| fig-cap: "Residuals by factor, main-effects model on log distance"
catapult |>
  pivot_longer(c(h, s, b, l, e), names_to = "factor", values_to = "level") |>
  mutate(factor = factor(factor_labels_coded[factor], levels = factor_labels_coded)) |>
  ggplot(aes(level, resid_log)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "gray60") +
  geom_point(color = "steelblue") +
  facet_wrap(~factor, nrow = 2) +
  labs(x = "Coded Factor Level", y = "Residual")
```

These plots still appear to have a slight "frown" on the graph (higher residuals in the center). However, the model is generally an improvement over the previous model and will be accepted as possibly the best that can be done without conducting a new experiment designed to fit a quadratic model.

**Step 5: Use the results to answer the questions in your experimental objectives**

*Final step: Predict the settings that should be used to obtain desired distances*

Based on the analyses and plots, we can select factor settings that maximize the log-transformed distance. Translating from "-1", "0", and "+1" back to the actual factor settings, we have: band height at "0" or 3.5 inches; start angle at "0" or 10 degrees; number of rubber bands at "1" or 2 bands; arm length at "1" or 4 inches; and stop angle at "0" or 80 degrees.

::: {.callout-note}
NIST's own factor descriptions above (and our verified `CATAPULT.DAT` data) put the coded "0" (centerpoint) level at 4.00 inches for band height and 62 degrees for stop angle, not 3.5 inches or 80 degrees. The value 80 is actually the *high* ("+1") level for stop angle. Reading the main effects plot below using the actual recorded levels, the optimal settings are: band height near 4.0 inches (level "0"), start angle at 10 degrees (level "0"), 2 rubber bands (level "+1"), arm length at 4 inches (level "+1"), and stop angle at 62 degrees (level "0") -- all five factors set to whichever level maximizes mean log(distance) in the plot below.
:::

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| label: fig-pri-472-maineffects
#| fig-cap: "Main effects plot"
main_eff <- catapult |>
  pivot_longer(c(height, start, bands, length, stop), names_to = "factor", values_to = "level") |>
  group_by(factor, level) |>
  summarise(mean_log = mean(log_distance), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(factor = factor(factor_labels_raw[factor], levels = factor_labels_raw))

grand_mean_log <- mean(catapult$log_distance)

ggplot(main_eff, aes(factor(level), mean_log, group = 1)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = grand_mean_log, color = "#D60021", linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_line(color = "steelblue") +
  geom_point(color = "steelblue", size = 2) +
  facet_wrap(~factor, nrow = 1, scales = "free_x") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Mean log(Distance)")
```

*"Confirmation" runs were successful*

In the confirmatory runs that followed the experiment, the team was successful at hitting all three targets, but did not hit them all five times. The model discovery and fitting process, as illustrated in this analysis, is often an iterative process.
